desc:
A grid matrix contains only 0 and 1. Count the rectangles (sub-grids of consecutive rows and consecutive columns, with at least one cell) in which every cell is 1. Rectangles at different positions are counted separately, even if they have the same size.

Example: [[1,0,1],[1,1,0],[1,1,0]] has 13 such rectangles: 6 single cells, 4 vertical dominoes... in total 13 once all sizes are added up (6 cells, 3 two-cell columns/rows pieces plus one 2 by 2 and further 3-cell and 4-cell/6-cell ones).
constraints: All rows have the same length
hints: Count rectangles by their bottom-right corner instead of all at once. For a fixed corner cell, how many rectangles end there?

With h[c] = number of consecutive ones above and including each cell of the current row, the number of rectangles with bottom-right corner in column c is the sum over left edges l ≤ c of min(h[l..c]).
That sum can be kept with a monotonic stack: if p is the nearest column to the left with h[p] < h[c], then cnt[c] = cnt[p] + h[c] * (c - p) (or h[c] * (c + 1) when there is no such column).
editorial: Process the grid row by row, updating h[c], the height of the column of ones that ends at the current row. Every all-ones rectangle has a unique bottom-right corner (r, c). For a left edge l the rectangle can be any height from 1 up to min(h[l..c]), so the number of rectangles at that corner is cnt[c] = sum over l ≤ c of min(h[l..c]).

Let p be the nearest column left of c with h[p] < h[c]. For left edges l in (p, c] the minimum is exactly h[c], contributing h[c] * (c - p); for left edges at or before p the minimum is the same as at corner p, contributing cnt[p]. A stack of increasing heights finds p in amortised O(1). Add cnt[c] over all cells to get the answer. Total time O(R * C), extra space O(C). The result is at most (80*81/2)2, which fits in 32 bits.
